terms.meaning: The organ that makes laws. From French "Parler" and Latin "Parliamentum", to talk or discuss.
The organ that carries out laws. From medieval Latin "Exsequi", to carry out.
The organ that interprets laws and gives justice. From Latin "Justitia".
A legislature with one house is unicameral; with two houses, bicameral.
A court order issued to protect a citizen's rights.
The court's power to check whether laws and orders follow the Constitution, and strike them down if not.

items.name: Nicknames of the legislature
items.formula: Barometer of public opinion, mirror of public opinion, law making factory.
items.example: It is the first organ of government.

items.name: Legislatures of other countries
items.formula: Maldives: Majlis. Germany: Bundestag. Israel: Knesset. France: National Assembly. Denmark: Folketing.

items.name: What the legislature does
items.formula: Makes and amends laws, forms the government, amends the Constitution, raises public grievances.
items.example: The party with a majority forms the government.

items.name: Countries with one house
items.formula: Greece, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Portugal, New Zealand.
items.example: It avoids repeated debates and saves money.

items.name: Two-house legislatures
items.formula: India: Lok Sabha (lower) and Rajya Sabha (upper). England: House of Commons and House of Lords.
items.example: Bicameralism began in England by historical accident.

items.name: Executive in the narrow and broad sense
items.formula: Narrow: the chief executive and advisers (India's President and Cabinet). Broad: everyone who carries out laws, down to clerks.
items.example: It is called the administrative organ.

items.name: Garner's definition of the executive
items.formula: The organ that carries out the state's will expressed through the legislature, Constitution and courts.
items.example: Willoughby: it sees that laws are carried out.

items.name: Nominal and real executive
items.formula: Nominal: power used in the head of state's name (India's President, Britain's monarch). Real: the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
items.example: In India the real power is with the Cabinet.

items.name: Parliamentary and presidential executive
items.formula: Parliamentary: chosen by and answerable to the legislature (India). Presidential: elected directly, not answerable to it (America).
items.example: In America one person is head of both state and government.

items.name: Single, plural, political and permanent executive
items.formula: Single: powers with the centre (England). Plural: shared among many (Switzerland).
items.example: Political: elected for a fixed term. Permanent: civil servants serving until retirement.

items.name: John Rawls on the judiciary
items.formula: It protects citizens' rights, punishes criminals, upholds justice and protects the innocent.
items.example: It is called the security-guard of the nation.

items.name: Why the judiciary matters
items.formula: Protects laws, rights and freedom; keeps order; builds trust that all are equal before law.
items.example: It stops the government overstepping its powers.

items.name: Unified and federal judiciary
items.formula: Unified: one chain of courts, Supreme Court down to magistrates (India, Canada). Federal: separate courts for centre and states (USA, Switzerland).
items.example: In India the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal.

items.name: Functions of the judiciary
items.formula: Interpreting laws, giving judgements, issuing writs, giving advice, judicial review.
items.example: India's courts can advise the government; America's don't.

mistakes.text: Legislature makes laws, executive carries them out, judiciary interprets and protects them.
India's President is the nominal executive; the real power lies with the Prime Minister's Cabinet.
Ministers are the political executive and change with elections; civil servants are the permanent executive.
